title: Same choice, two ways to write it
idea: You can often swap which outcome is the if and which is the else by flipping the comparison. Both can be correct.

exercises.explanation: Version B flips the question to score < 60 and swaps the two outcomes. Both versions give the same results.
70 < 60 is False, so the else branch runs: Pass. Same answer as Version A would give.
40 < 60 is True, so the if branch runs: Fail. Flipping the condition also flips which branch holds each outcome.

exercises.prompt: If you flip the comparison, you must also swap the two branches to keep the same meaning.
exercises.explanation: Yes. Change >= 60 to < 60 AND swap Pass/Fail. Flip one without the other and the meaning reverses.

exercises.prompt: Match each condition to the branch that should hold 'Pass' to keep the Pass/Fail rule correct.

pairs.right: Pass goes in the if branch
Pass goes in the else branch

exercises.explanation: With >= 60, true means pass, so Pass is under if. With < 60, true means fail, so Pass moves to else.

exercises.prompt: Which comparison is the opposite of >= ?
exercises.explanation: 'At least' (>=) flips to 'below' (<). They split all numbers between them with no overlap and no gap.

exercises.prompt: Which comparison is the opposite of == ?
exercises.explanation: 'Equal' (==) flips to 'different' (!=). If you swap branches, you can rewrite one as the other.
The opposite of >= 30 is < 30. With the condition flipped, 'Not hot' now sits in the if branch.

exercises.prompt: Why is it fine that one problem has two correct if/else versions?
options: As long as each case prints the right outcome, the wording of the condition is your choice
You must always check the true case first
exercises.explanation: Correctness is about the outcomes, not the exact phrasing. Pick whichever version reads most clearly to you.

exercises.prompt: What is the safe rule when flipping a condition?
options: Flip the comparison AND swap the two branches together
exercises.explanation: Change both together and the behaviour stays the same. Changing just one quietly reverses the logic.
